title: The Letter of Intent Isn't the Sale. The Months After It Decide Whether the Deal Survives.
excerpt: A signed letter of intent feels like the finish line, but due diligence is where deals actually collapse or get repriced. Here is what buyers really test, and how sellers protect the number they agreed to.
content:
Signing a letter of intent feels like the sale is done. The number is on paper, the buyer has nodded, and for the first time in months an owner can picture life on the other side of settlement. It is a natural moment to relax.

It is also the point where a meaningful share of deals that looked certain either collapse outright or get renegotiated down to a number nobody would have accepted at the outset. A letter of intent is usually non-binding on price and conditional on due diligence. In the way it feels, the deal is done. In the way it actually works, almost nothing has been agreed yet.

What changes between signing and settlement is not the business. It is how closely everything the owner has said about the business gets checked, and how well the business holds up once someone else is doing the checking.

Why the Agreement Stage Feels Safer Than It Is

A letter of intent, or heads of agreement, typically sets out price, structure and a timeline, then makes nearly all of it conditional on the buyer completing due diligence to their satisfaction. For a transaction in the small to mid-market range, that window usually runs four to twelve weeks, longer again if bank or investor approval sits on the buyer's side of the deal. During that time the buyer's accountants, lawyers and sometimes an operational advisor go through the business in a level of detail most owners have never experienced. The relief that comes with signing is real, but it is relief based on what the buyer has seen so far, not on what they are about to find. Owners who have sold once before tend to describe this stage differently the second time around, less as a celebration and more as the start of the actual negotiation.

What Due Diligence Actually Tests

The pattern we typically see is not dishonesty. It is normal business practice that was never built to survive this kind of scrutiny. Addbacks that made sense to the owner and their bookkeeper do not always hold up when a buyer's accountant asks for evidence behind each one. A customer that looked like a single relationship on the profit and loss turns out to be two contracts with very different renewal terms. Management reporting that was accurate enough to run the business month to month does not always reconcile cleanly against the tax return a buyer's advisor is comparing it to, and the gap between the two numbers becomes the first thing a buyer's team raises once they find it. None of this means the business is weaker than the owner believed. It usually means the business was run for itself, not for a stranger trying to verify every figure inside a six week window.

Retrading Is the Outcome Most Owners Don't See Coming

A collapsed deal is the outcome owners fear, but the more common result is retrading, where the buyer comes back partway through due diligence and asks for a lower price, an earnout, or extra warranties to cover whatever made them uncomfortable. It rarely looks like bad faith from the buyer's side. It looks like a buyer protecting themselves against uncertainty the seller could have removed before the business ever went to market. Once a number has been floated and half accepted in an owner's mind, a reduction two months later stings far more than the same number would have if it had simply been the opening position. A valuation built on numbers that already reconcile the way a buyer's advisor will want them to gives a seller far less room to be retraded against, because there is nothing left for due diligence to discover that the seller did not already know and disclose.

Preparing the Business Before a Buyer Ever Sees It

This is the exact gap a Vendor Due Diligence Pack is built to close: a buyer-ready financial and commercial information set, prepared and verified before the business goes to market, so the questions that would otherwise surface six weeks into a live deal are already answered in writing. It will not remove every question a buyer asks. It removes the kind of surprise that turns a confident buyer cautious halfway through a transaction, and that is usually the difference between a deal that settles on the agreed terms and one that does not.

For many Brisbane business owners weighing up a sale in the next one to three years, the real work happens well before the first buyer conversation, in getting the numbers, the contracts and the story of the business ready to survive someone else's scrutiny. That is a different exercise to running the business day to day, and it rewards starting earlier than feels necessary. If a sale is somewhere on the horizon, a conversation now costs nothing and buys time the deal itself will not give you later. Book a discovery call to talk through where the business stands today.

faqs.q: What causes a business sale to fall through after a letter of intent is signed?
faqs.a: Most collapses trace back to something a buyer finds during due diligence that was never flagged earlier, often unreconciled addbacks, undisclosed customer concentration or management reporting that does not match the tax figures. The business is rarely the real problem. The surprise is. A business that has already reconciled its numbers before going to market gives a buyer far less reason to walk away partway through.

faqs.q: Is a letter of intent legally binding in an Australian business sale?
faqs.a: Usually only in parts. A letter of intent typically locks in exclusivity and confidentiality, but leaves price and final terms conditional on due diligence. That is deliberate. It gives both sides room to walk away or renegotiate if what due diligence uncovers does not match what was represented at the outset, which is exactly the period a seller should prepare for before it starts.

faqs.q: What is vendor due diligence and why would a seller commission one?
faqs.a: Vendor due diligence is a buyer-ready pack of financial and commercial information prepared by the seller before a business goes to market, rather than compiled under pressure once a buyer asks. It answers the questions a buyer's advisor would otherwise raise mid deal, which protects both the price and the timeline. Our Vendor Due Diligence Pack is built around exactly this gap.

faqs.q: What do buyers check most closely during financial due diligence?
faqs.a: Buyers and their advisors focus on whether reported profit holds up once addbacks are tested, whether customer and contract concentration is as diversified as it appeared, and whether monthly management figures reconcile against the tax return. A valuation built on verified numbers rather than owner estimates tends to survive this scrutiny with far fewer adjustments.

faqs.q: How long does due diligence usually take for an SME sale in Australia?
faqs.a: For most transactions under thirty million dollars, due diligence runs four to twelve weeks, longer where bank or investor approval is part of the buyer's funding. The length matters less than what happens inside it. A seller who has already reconciled their numbers tends to move through the window faster and with fewer price conversations than one discovering gaps in real time.

faqs.q: Can a buyer renegotiate the price after a letter of intent is signed?
faqs.a: Yes, and it happens more often than outright collapse. Retrading, where a buyer asks for a lower price, an earnout or extra warranties partway through due diligence, is usually a response to something unresolved rather than bad faith. The pattern we see most often is preventable, because most of what triggers it was already sitting in the business before the buyer ever looked.
